narration: The eleventh-century antlers of Abbots Bromley.
This is the Abbots Bromley Horn Dance, dating from the medieval and seventeenth-century periods.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The earliest written mention of the Abbots Bromley Horn Dance appears in Robert Plot's 1686 Natural History of Staffordshire, though a 1532 record notes a hobby-horse performance at Abbots Bromley as an ancient custom.
In 1976, radiocarbon dating of one of the reindeer horns revealed a date of 1065.
Various explanations for the dance's origin have been proposed—including pagan rituals, winter solstice fertility rites, and hunting customs—but concrete evidence is lacking.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance takes place annually on Wakes Monday, the day following the first Sunday after September 4.
Historically, it occurred during the Christmas and New Year period and served to raise money for church repairs and the parish poor.
It is frequently associated with folk interpretations of fertility and hunting rights, though historians note a lack of direct documentary evidence for these meanings.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is composed of two main figures.
In the first figure, the dancers process around in a circle before turning and circling back.
In the second figure, the dancers face off in two rows, dancing together and apart before crossing over, turning around, and returning to their original places.
Watch for the Horn Circle and Row Cross-Over.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by a musician playing an accordion (historically a violin) and a youth with a triangle.
Dancers holding the hobby horse's jaw and the bow and arrow also use them as percussion instruments to keep time.
Listen for the accordion, triangle, jaw of hobby horse, and bow and arrow percussion.
The pulse is 4/4.
A steady country-dance air plays on an accordion, accompanied by the sharp strike of a triangle and percussion from the hobby horse's jaw, maintaining a measured, plodding pulse.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Until the 1880s, dancers wore everyday clothing decorated with ribbons.
Subsequently, mock-medieval costumes were designed, evolving into modern green or red jackets with green breeches bearing an oak leaf pattern.
The hobby horse is constructed in the tourney style with a head and frame covered by cloth.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures documented in the history of the dance include Robert Plot, who provided the first detailed description in 1686; Cecil Sharp, who recorded the dance figures and music in 1911; and local families such as the Bentleys and Fowells, who have historically led the tradition.

While the authentic horn dance must remain within the parish of Abbots Bromley according to tradition, adapted versions have been performed outside the village by the English Folk Dance and Song Society, the Thaxted Morris Men, and international groups in America using separate replica horns.
The dance is connected to broader English morris and ritual animal disguise traditions, sharing historical performance contexts with winter guising customs across the Midlands.

The setting spans the parish of Abbots Bromley, beginning at St Nicholas's Church, moving through the marketplace, and visiting locations such as Blithfield Hall.

A scan from a print of a 35mm transparency which I took at the Abbots Bromley Horn Dance in Abbots Bromley, Staffordshire, England in the mid 1970s. It shows the original medieval hobby horse (sitting down to take a rest in the early evening after a full day's dancing). Soon after this, a new hobby horse was carved, with a more "realistic" head.
